sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Defining Weight-Loss-Independent Hepatic Effects of Incretin-Based Therapies》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Post‐Randomization Subgrouping Does Not Establish Weight‐Loss Independence · dom71391-sec-0002-p1】The recent Phase 2 DD01 trial, a novel GLP‐1R/GCGR co‐agonist, illustrates the challenge. Its prespecified primary endpoint was the proportion of participants achieving at least 30% relative reduction in liver fat by MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI‐PDFF) at Week 12; body weight was an exploratory outcome and the < 5% weight‐loss subgroup analysis was post hoc [5]. After 12 weeks, mean body weight decreased by 3.8% with DD01 versus 0.4% with placebo and 14 (42%) of 33 DD01‐treated participants achieved at least 5% weight loss [5]. Hepatic benefits among participants losing < 5% of body weight are clinically encouraging and hypothesis‐generating, but this subgroup should not be interpreted as establishing causal independence from weight loss. Achieved weight change is a post‐randomization variable affected by treatment. Restricting an analysis to participants below an arbitrary weight‐loss threshold no longer preserves the original randomized comparison. Participants who remain below 5% weight loss after active treatment might differ from placebo participants meeting the same threshold in adherence, treatment exposure, baseline metabolic phenotype, appetite response, disease severity or other determinants of hepatic outcomes. Conditioning on a treatment‐affected variable can therefore introduce selection or collider bias, in which restricting on a variable influenced by both treatment and prognostic factors creates spurious associations between them [6]. Dichotomization also discards information: Participants losing 0.5% and 4.9% of body weight are assigned to the same category despite markedly different metabolic responses.

【A Framework for Future MASLD Trials · dom71391-sec-0004-p3】Third, post‐randomization weight‐loss subgroup analyses can remain clinically descriptive and useful, but should not be presented as proof of causal independence. If the scientific question specifically concerns people who would experience limited weight reduction irrespective of treatment assignment, principal‐stratum estimands are conceptually closer to this question than stratification according to observed weight loss. However, principal‐stratum estimands are rarely feasible in typical Phase 2 trials because they require strong assumptions, specialized methods and substantially larger sample sizes. The DD01 study, with only 33 participants assigned to active treatment, illustrates this limitation. Finally, causal and biological evidence should be triangulated. A persuasive claim of weight‐independent hepatic efficacy would ideally combine randomized treatment effects, formal mediation analyses, consistency across prespecified hepatic endpoints and time points and mechanistic or biomarker evidence supporting pathways beyond weight reduction. Useful correlative markers may include serial body weight, appetite or caloric‐intake measures, HbA1c, fasting glucose and insulin, serum lipids, adipokines, inflammatory markers, ALT and AST, ELF score, PRO‐C3, MRE and MRI‐PDFF. Discordance across outcomes might itself be informative. For example, a therapy whose effect on hepatic steatosis is predominantly weight mediated but whose effect on fibrosis is not could reveal clinically important biology that would be obscured by applying a single class‐wide label.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Defining Weight-Loss-Independent Hepatic Effects of Incretin-Based Therapies》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Post‐Randomization Subgrouping Does Not Establish Weight‐Loss Independence · dom71391-sec-0002-p1】The recent Phase 2 DD01 trial, a novel GLP‐1R/GCGR co‐agonist, illustrates the challenge. After 12 weeks, mean body weight decreased by 3.8% with DD01 versus 0.4% with placebo and 14 (42%) of 33 DD01‐treated participants achieved at least 5% weight loss [5]. Hepatic benefits among participants losing < 5% of body weight are clinically encouraging and hypothesis‐generating, but this subgroup should not be interpreted as establishing causal independence from weight loss. Restricting an analysis to participants below an arbitrary weight‐loss threshold no longer preserves the original randomized comparison. Participants who remain below 5% weight loss after active treatment might differ from placebo participants meeting the same threshold in adherence, treatment exposure, baseline metabolic phenotype, appetite response, disease severity or other determinants of hepatic outcomes. Conditioning on a treatment‐affected variable can therefore introduce selection or collider bias, in which restricting on a variable influenced by both treatment and prognostic factors creates spurious associations between them [6]. Dichotomization also discards information: Participants losing 0.5% and 4.9% of body weight are assigned to the same category despite markedly different metabolic responses.

【Weight Mediation Is Endpoint Specific · dom71391-sec-0003-p3】Biological evidence can support mechanistic plausibility but should not be conflated with causal mediation in humans. In mouse models resistant to GLP‐1R‐mediated weight loss, semaglutide still improved MASLD, whereas loss of GLP‐1Rs in liver sinusoidal endothelial cells substantially disrupted its hepatoprotective effects despite preserved weight reduction [9]. These findings support the biological plausibility of intrahepatic GLP‐1R‐dependent pathways in experimental models, although their relevance to weight‐independent hepatic effects in humans remains uncertain. Importantly, ‘not mediated by weight loss’ is not synonymous with ‘directly acting on the liver’. A putative weight‐independent component in humans could also operate through systemic or extrahepatic processes, including changes in glycaemia, insulin sensitivity, adipose‐tissue lipolysis, nutrient intake, glucagon signalling, systemic inflammation or inter‐organ communication [10] (Figure 1C). Thus, evidence for incomplete weight mediation should be viewed as hypothesis‐generating rather than as proof of a specific intrahepatic pathway.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Defining Weight-Loss-Independent Hepatic Effects of Incretin-Based Therapies》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【FIGURE 1 · dom71391-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 Causal framework for evaluating weight‐loss‐independent hepatic effects of incretin‐based therapies. (A) Incretin‐based therapies may improve liver outcomes through weight‐mediated and putative non‐weight‐mediated pathways; post‐randomization subgroup findings can be clinically descriptive but are not causal proof. (B) A more rigorous approach separates the total treatment effect into weight‐mediated and putative weight‐independent components using continuous weight modelling, causal mediation and endpoint‐specific analyses. (C) Candidate mediators and correlative biomarkers beyond body‐weight change include measures of glycaemia and insulin sensitivity, appetite and energy intake, adipose‐tissue lipid flux, and liver‐related biomarkers. These variables are illustrative; associations do not by themselves establish direct hepatic action. Abbreviations: ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; CAP, controlled attenuation parameter; ELF, enhanced liver fibrosis test; HbA1c, glycated haemoglobin; LSM, liver stiffness measurement; MRE, magnetic resonance elastography; MRI‐PDFF, magnetic resonance imaging–proton density fat fraction; PRO‐C3, N‐terminal propeptide of type III collagen.
